strengths: The paper identifies a practically important failure mode in text-to-CAD systems: missing or conflicting dimensions should often trigger clarification rather than silent guessing. Applying proactive clarification to CAD appears relatively original, although the underlying two-agent/SFT recipe is straightforward.

The system is clearly decomposed into clarification, specification correction, and code generation. Full prompts, training objectives, data statistics, ambiguity categories, failure analysis, and an interaction-protocol ablation make the method unusually easy to understand.

The evaluation is broad within the proposed setting. It includes fixed-coder comparisons, strong proprietary and open-model baselines, two user simulators, geometry and execution metrics, qualitative examples, and a 100-example human-centered evaluation. The same-coder results support the claim that the trained clarifier improves downstream generation.

The reported gains are substantial: with ProCAD-coder fixed, replacing Claude Sonnet 4.5 with ProCAD-clarifier reduces mean CD from 2.69 to 0.63 and invalidity from 2.3% to 0.9% on the synthetic test set. The paper also reports informative remaining weaknesses, especially the drop from 98.2% success for one ambiguity to 77.1% for two.
weaknesses: The central robustness evidence is largely circular and distribution-matched. GPT-5-mini generates the canonical descriptions, constructs the ambiguities, simulates users, and judges interaction quality. Samples are additionally selected using ProCAD-coder according to whether the perturbation increases its Chamfer distance. This produces a benchmark tailored to the exact perturbation process, coder, and judge used by the method, so it does not convincingly establish robustness to naturally occurring ambiguity.

The human-centered evaluation does not adequately close this gap. Annotators are shown the canonical prompt and reference image and asked to manufacture ambiguous rewrites, rather than contributing natural CAD requests arising from genuine design intent. Only 100 examples are used, with no uncertainty intervals, significance tests, annotator counts, recruitment details, agreement statistics, or breakdown by ambiguity type. In this evaluation, ProCAD and Claude also have identical invalidity rates (12.2%), while the median-CD difference is small (0.11 versus 0.09); the large mean improvement may therefore depend on a few severe errors.

The evaluated ambiguity space is narrow: omissions of one or two dimensions and explicit conflicting values. It excludes many realistic cases such as ambiguous topology, feature references, units, tolerances, coordinate frames, manufacturability constraints, and vague relational language. The canonical prompts are generated directly from code using a fixed three-part template, making both coding and clarification substantially more structured than unconstrained user input. Claims about real-world CAD robustness should consequently be narrowed.

Important experimental details are unclear. The paper does not state whether ambiguous train/test examples are split by underlying CAD shape, leaving possible geometry or canonical-prompt leakage. It also omits random seeds, decoding settings, exact Chamfer sampling and normalization, treatment of invalid programs in CD aggregation, variability across training runs, and confidence intervals. The claimed public code/data link is absent in the submitted manuscript, although the supplied prompts improve partial reproducibility.

Some comparisons support weaker conclusions than claimed. Better zero-shot performance on the new descriptions shows that they are easier for a particular code generator to consume, but does not by itself prove that they are more human-like or intrinsically higher quality. The LLM preference study uses the same GPT-5-mini family involved in data creation and shows pronounced order sensitivity for clarity (98.4% versus 66.0%), while no independent human dataset-quality assessment is provided.

The formal MDP and reward formulation are mostly motivational: the proposed method performs supervised imitation under a fixed two-round protocol and never optimizes the stated Chamfer/communication reward. Thus the methodological originality is moderate, and terms such as “optimal policy” and broad agentic framing overstate what is actually trained.

Presentation is generally polished, but there are consequential inconsistencies: Table 4 calls all 2,469 test prompts ambiguous, whereas Table 8 reports that 1,000 are unambiguous. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion and uses a generic impact statement despite emphasizing possible manufacturing failures. Human-participant procedures, consent/compensation, and risks of relying on geometrically plausible but engineering-unsafe CAD outputs are not discussed.

strengths: Originality/significance: Applying proactive clarification before text-to-CAD synthesis is a sensible and useful direction. Separating specification auditing from code generation could improve practical CAD interfaces.

Soundness: The evaluation includes executable-code invalidity, mean and median Chamfer distance, interaction-quality measures, multiple coding-agent configurations, an alternative user simulator, protocol ablations, qualitative cases, and a small human-centered study.

The curated text-to-CadQuery pipeline is a potentially valuable contribution. Starting from executable programs and checking whether descriptions permit geometry reconstruction is more principled than relying only on stylistic text-quality judgments.
Presentation: The overall pipeline, training targets, prompts, ambiguity categories, and principal comparisons are explained clearly, and the appendices disclose useful prompts and failure analyses.
weaknesses: Soundness: The main evaluation is strongly circular. GPT-5-mini generates the clean descriptions, creates and self-refines the synthetic ambiguities, supplies simulated user answers, and judges important outcomes. Training and testing therefore reward conformity to one synthetic pipeline rather than establish robustness to naturally occurring ambiguity.

The claimed real-user validation is not ecologically convincing. Annotators are shown a synthetic precise prompt and reference image and asked to deliberately rewrite it ambiguously; this is not a sample of genuine user requests or naturally arising misunderstandings. Only 100 source examples are used, with no uncertainty estimates or statistical tests.

Baseline comparisons are materially asymmetric. ProCAD is fine-tuned directly on the dataset's description style and prescribed corruption process, whereas Claude, GPT-4o-mini, and base Qwen are largely prompted off the shelf. Thus the reported superiority to frontier models does not isolate the framework, model training, or data-distribution advantage.

The formal MDP and reward are not actually optimized. Training is supervised maximum likelihood, lambda is unused, and the assertion that an optimal interaction reduces to two rounds follows only after assuming users always know every requested value and treating rounds as the key cost. This does not justify broader claims about minimal burden or optimal interaction.

Critical metric details are absent: mesh normalization and point sampling for Chamfer distance, treatment of invalid programs in CD aggregates, decoding settings, repeated-run variability, and confidence intervals are not reported. These omissions make the large headline percentage improvements difficult to interpret or reproduce.

Dataset and split documentation is insufficient. Exact UID splits and leakage controls between coder/clarifier datasets are not supplied, and ambiguity cases are selected precisely because ProCAD-coder fails by a threshold and tenfold CD ratio. This conditions the benchmark on one component's failure modes and may distort comparisons.

The human study lacks essential reporting: annotator counts, expertise criteria, assignment scheme, agreement, compensation, consent/ethics procedure, and uncertainty are omitted. Table 6's percentages are also not readily reconcilable with the stated 100-example setup.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies. Table 4 is captioned as containing 2,469 ambiguous prompts although Table 8 says 1,000 are unambiguous; nearby prose and Table 1 disagree on several zero-shot invalidity values; and “efficiency” measures agreement with synthetic ground-truth questions rather than actual communication cost.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the public-release claim: the manuscript provides no usable repository link, exact data/splits, seeds, inference parameters, complete optimization configuration, or executable evaluation protocol. Reliance on proprietary, time-versioned GPT and Claude services further increases reproducibility risk.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. The conclusion briefly calls for real-world interaction data, but it does not confront the benchmark circularity, baseline asymmetry, or manufacturing risks of dimensionally incorrect CAD. The generic impact statement dismisses potential consequences, and no responsible protocol for the human evaluation is documented.

Overall, the idea and preliminary results have merit, but the evidence does not support the central claims of robust real-user clarification, minimal interaction, or superiority to frontier systems. Substantial benchmark redesign, genuinely natural human evaluation, fair trained baselines, statistical reporting, and a reproducible release are needed before acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The central result is supported by substantial evaluation. On 2,469 test cases, ProCAD-clarifier paired with ProCAD-coder attains mean CD 0.63×10^-3 and 0.9% invalidity, compared with 2.69×10^-3 and 2.3% for Claude Sonnet 4.5 as clarifier. Changing the user simulator from GPT-5-mini to Claude Haiku preserves the advantage.

Significance: Detecting missing or conflicting dimensions before code synthesis addresses a practical failure mode that conventional one-shot and post-hoc refinement systems largely neglect. The separation between clarification and coding is useful, interpretable, and modular.

Originality: Applying a trained proactive clarification policy to text-to-CAD, together with supervision for minimal targeted questions, is a meaningful and relatively novel formulation even though the underlying two-agent and SFT techniques are standard.

The paper includes a valuable human-centered evaluation on 100 examples. With human-written ambiguities, human responses, and expert scoring, ProCAD remains strongest in efficiency, resolution, and mean CD, partially validating transfer beyond fully synthetic interactions.

The controlled coder experiment is persuasive: using identical shapes, splits, backbone, and fine-tuning settings, the proposed descriptions substantially outperform Text-CAD and JSON-Distill. This supports the useful finding that specification quality is a major text-to-CAD bottleneck.

Presentation and reproducibility are generally strong: the method is clearly organized, full system and judge prompts are supplied, training hyperparameters and dataset counts are reported, failure cases are analyzed, and the interaction-protocol ablation exposes the quality/latency tradeoff.
weaknesses: Soundness: Most of the main benchmark is synthetic and highly coupled to the proposed pipeline. GPT-5-mini generates ambiguities and user answers, participates in constructing and verifying the source descriptions, and judges interaction quality. Switching only the answer simulator to Claude Haiku does not test genuinely different ambiguity distributions.

The ambiguous benchmark is filtered to retain cases where ProCAD-coder performs poorly on the corrupted prompt and at least ten times better on the original prompt. Conditioning test selection on the same downstream coder used in the primary system can inflate the apparent benefit of clarification and limits conclusions about general robustness.

The human study is encouraging but under-specified and small. The paper does not report annotator counts per example, recruitment, expertise distribution, compensation, agreement, blinding, or uncertainty intervals. Participants also rewrite already synthetic, template-like specifications while seeing the reference prompt and image, rather than supplying naturally occurring CAD requests.

Evaluation omits confidence intervals or significance tests despite some close results. Chamfer distance and executable validity also do not assess important CAD properties such as topology, feature-tree correctness, editability, constraint semantics, or manufacturability.

Presentation: The MDP and reward formulation suggests direct optimization of geometric fidelity and communication cost, but the clarifier is actually trained by supervised likelihood on synthetic trajectories; the reward is conceptual rather than an optimized objective. Table 4 is also captioned as containing 2,469 ambiguous prompts although Table 8 shows that 1,000 are unambiguous.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied prompts: exact decoding settings, random seeds, mesh sampling/normalization for Chamfer distance, detailed human-evaluation instructions, and expert adjudication procedures are not reported. The manuscript states that code and data are public, but the displayed link is empty in this version.

The claimed real-world scope is broader than the evidence. Data originate from DeepCAD/CAD-Recode and cover only two controlled ambiguity types—missing and conflicting dimensions—while real requests may involve vague intent, units, references, tolerances, infeasible constraints, feature relations, and evolving user preferences.

Ethics and limitations are treated too briefly. The generic impact statement does not address risks from dimensionally incorrect CAD used in manufacturing, appropriate human verification, dataset/code licensing, or the treatment of human annotators. The paper acknowledges synthetic-user limitations, but a more explicit safety and deployment discussion is warranted.
